structure.title: The Hebrew scriptures
structure.text: Origins, law, national histories, poetry, and prophecy offer different forms of remembering and addressing God.

structure.title: The New Testament
structure.text: Gospels and Acts lead into letters and Revelation. Narrative, correspondence, and visionary writing require different kinds of attention.

people.name: Covenant
people.text: A binding relationship with obligations and promises.

people.name: Israel
people.text: Both a people and a central subject of the scriptures.

people.name: Jesus
people.text: The central figure of the New Testament.

context.title: A collection of books
context.text: These writings arose in different settings and speak in different voices. A lament, a law, and a letter are doing different things.
context.takeaway: Identify the kind of text before generalising.

context.title: Reused stories
context.text: Later writers revisit creation, Exodus, kingship, and covenant. An apparent new beginning often carries the language of an earlier deliverance or failure.
context.takeaway: Repetition can reinterpret what came before.

notice.text: Attend to arguments addressed to God.
notice.why: Faith can include protest and demands for an answer.

notice.text: Distinguish a character's action from its narrative setting.
notice.why: Recording conduct does not automatically endorse it.

opening: A brother kills his brother. A people escapes slavery and begins quarrelling in the wilderness. A righteous man loses everything and demands an answer from God. Centuries later, a teacher tells his listeners to love their enemies, and is executed. The Bible gathers stories, laws, songs, accusations, and promises that have given generations their language for suffering and hope. Read together, these writings are more unruly than their familiar quotations suggest: even the faithful argue, and some of the fiercest arguments are addressed to God.
